cards.text: Paul is writing to the believers in Rome, and he's just said a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Now he calls his star witness: Abraham, the forefather of Israel. If ANYBODY could've earned it, friend, it's this man.

cards.question: Paul says that if Abraham was justified by works, he would have something to boast about before God.

cards.text: So Paul goes straight to the Scripture to settle it. It says one thing about Abraham was credited to him as righteousness.

cards.question: According to the Scripture Paul quotes, what was credited to Abraham as righteousness?

cards.text: Now Paul pulls out an everyday picture: a worker and his wages. Friend, NOBODY opens their paycheck and cries, “You shouldn't have! You're too generous!”

cards.question: Paul says a worker's wages are credited not as a gift but as an ___.

cards.text: But then Paul flips it. Picture someone who doesn't work for it at all, but simply believes in God.

cards.question: Paul describes the God this person believes in. Who does Paul say God justifies?
For the person who doesn't work but believes, Paul says their faith is credited as righteousness.

cards.text: Then Paul brings a second witness: David, king of Israel, who talks about how blessed someone is when God credits righteousness to them apart from works. Abraham AND David? Paul didn't come to argue, friend, he came with RECEIPTS.

cards.question: In the words Paul quotes from David, what has happened to the sins of the blessed?
David says the blessed man is the one whose sin the Lord will still count against him later.

cards.text: Now Paul asks a sharp question: is this blessing only for the circumcised, or for the uncircumcised too? He points right back to Abraham, whose faith was credited to him as righteousness.

cards.question: Paul asks when Abraham's faith was credited to him as righteousness. When was it?

answers.text: On the day of his circumcision

cards.text: Faith came first, and circumcision came after, as a seal of the righteousness Abraham already had. It's like a wedding ring, friend: it doesn't make you married, it shows you already are.

cards.question: Because of that timing, Paul says Abraham is the father of all who ___ but are not circumcised.
Paul says Abraham is also the father of the circumcised. What else marks them as his children?

answers.text: Living in the land of Canaan

cards.text: Now Paul talks about God's promise that Abraham and his offspring would be heir of the world. Heir of the WORLD, friend. Meanwhile the biggest thing anybody ever handed me was a spot in the back of a junk drawer.

cards.question: Paul says this promise to Abraham was not given through the law. What was it given through?

answers.text: The righteousness that comes by faith

cards.text: Then Paul plays it the other way. What if the heirs were the people who live by the law?

cards.question: If those who live by the law are the heirs, Paul says faith is useless and the promise is ___.

cards.text: Then Paul gives his reason, and part of it is this: where there is no law, there is no transgression. No rule, no rule-breaking.

cards.question: Paul says the law brings wrath.
Paul says the promise comes by ___, so that it may rest on ___.
Paul says the promise comes by faith so that it may rest on grace and be guaranteed. Who does he say it is guaranteed to?

answers.text: Only those who keep the law

cards.text: Then Paul says it plain: Abraham is the father of us all. That's one BIG family reunion, friend, and somebody's gonna need a LOT more cookie boxes.
Paul backs it up with what is written, where God tells Abraham, “I have made you a father of many nations.” And Abraham is our father in the presence of the God he believed.

cards.question: Paul describes the God Abraham believed in. What does Paul say this God does?

cards.text: Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed, and became the father of many nations, just as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.” Against hope... in hope. Read that one again slow, friend.
Abraham is about a hundred years old, and Sarah, his wife, has a lifeless womb. A HUNDRED, friend, and I need to sit down after stamping one batch.

cards.question: Abraham ignored how old his body was so that his faith wouldn't weaken.
Facing the promise of God, Abraham was ___ in his faith and gave glory to God.
Abraham was fully persuaded that he had earned what God promised him.

cards.text: That's why “it was credited to him as righteousness.” And Paul says the words “it was credited to him” weren't written only for Abraham.

cards.question: Paul says those words were written for others too. Who does he say righteousness will be credited to?

answers.text: Those who believe in Him who raised Jesus
Those who keep every part of the law
Those born into Abraham's family line

cards.text: And Paul ends right where it all points: Jesus our Lord. He was delivered over to death for our trespasses.

cards.question: Jesus was delivered over to death for our trespasses. What does Paul say He was raised to life for?

findings.problem: The opening card cites Romans 3:28-4:1. That range reaches outside stop 1's range (Romans 4:1-12) and outside the passage. The card also says Paul is writing to the believers in Rome. That fact comes from Romans 1 and has no reference, and the single verses field can't cite it without stretching the range.
findings.question: When an opening card gives context from outside the passage, such as the verse just before it or a letter's author and readers, should it cite those verses? If so, how, given the 'no wider and no narrower' range rule and the stop's own verse range?

findings.problem: "It says one thing about Abraham was credited to him as righteousness" is garbled and hard to read. It also has none of Papa Dorin's voice, so the moment falls flat as setup for the next choice card.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The two right answers, faith and grace, could reasonably be placed in either blank. A baker could argue that "the promise comes by grace, so that it may rest on faith" is right, but the card marks that placement as wrong.
findings.question: On a two-blank card, must the right answers be words that can't be argued to fit each other's blank? Or is a swapped placement of two right answers acceptable?

findings.problem: The joke "A HUNDRED, friend, and I need to sit down after stamping one batch" contrasts Papa Dorin's tiredness with Abraham's age. That suggests Abraham was still going strong at a hundred. Romans 4:19 says Abraham acknowledged the decrepitness of his body. The comparison doesn't share the core action of the fact and points the opposite way from the text.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: Romans 4:21 is a key line of the passage: Abraham was fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised. It only appears as a false true-or-false statement about Abraham thinking he had earned the promise. No story card ever tells what Abraham was actually persuaded of, so the baker can leave Prep without that detail.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.
